title: 5. Regulatory and Compliance
subtitle: Regulation · RegTech · RBI Sandbox · AML · KYC · Tax issues
subject: FinTech

sections.heading: Introduction and Learning Objectives
sections.html:
Trust is the currency of finance. This module explains how FinTech is regulated in India and abroad, how RegTech helps firms and supervisors, the role of the RBI and its sandbox, the compliance pillars of AML and KYC, and the tax issues for Assessment Year 2026-27.

Learning objectives

  • Describe the FinTech regulatory framework in India
  • Explain RegTech, SupTech and the ecosystem
  • Discuss financial inclusion, adoption and regulatory challenges
  • Explain the RBI's roles and the Regulatory Sandbox
  • Apply AML and KYC concepts
  • Summarise FinTech tax issues for AY 2026-27

sections.heading: 5.1 FinTech Regulation: Framework
sections.html:
FinTech regulation must balance three objectives that can pull in different directions: innovation and competition, consumer protection and financial stability. Arner et al. argue that regulators now need to move from rule-based, entity-focused supervision to approaches that use data and technology themselves [1]. Zetzsche et al. add that data-driven finance blurs the lines between financial and technology companies and raises new questions about data governance [2].

Table 1. Regulatory architecture for FinTech in India

RegulatorDomainKey law or instrument
Reserve Bank of India (RBI)Banking, payments, NBFCs, digital lendingRBI Act, 1934; Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 [3]
SEBISecurities markets, investment advisers, mutual fundsSEBI Act, 1992; Investment Advisers Regulations, 2013 [4]
IRDAIInsurance and InsurTechInsurance Act, 1938; IRDA Act, 1999
PFRDAPension schemesPFRDA Act, 2013
IFSCAFinancial services in GIFT CityIFSCA Act, 2019
MeitY and CERT-InCyber-security and dataIT Act, 2000 [5]; DPDP Act, 2023 [6]

Regulatory approaches. Same risk, same regulation holds that similar activities face similar rules regardless of who performs them. Activity-based regulation focuses on what is done, whereas entity-based regulation focuses on who does it. Principles-based rules set outcomes, while rules-based approaches prescribe procedures. Innovation facilitators such as sandboxes and innovation hubs help regulators learn from new products.

Licence categories relevant to FinTech in India

Table 2. Common licences and authorisations

Entity typeAuthorityWhat it permits
Payment aggregator or gatewayRBICollecting and settling payments for merchants
Prepaid payment instrument issuerRBIIssuing wallets and prepaid instruments
NBFC (including NBFC-P2P and NBFC-MFI)RBILending and related financial services
NBFC-Account AggregatorRBIConsent-based financial data sharing
Payments bank and small finance bankRBILimited-scope banking services
Stock broker and investment adviserSEBISecurities trading and advice
Insurance intermediaryIRDAIDistribution of insurance products

International comparison

Regulators abroad have adopted varied responses. The United Kingdom's Financial Conduct Authority launched one of the first regulatory sandboxes and published lessons learned, noting benefits such as shorter time to market and improved access to funding for tested firms [7]. The European Union has addressed payment services and open banking through its payment services directives and has moved on crypto-asset rules. Singapore combines licensing with active promotion of innovation. These approaches are useful reference points when evaluating India's choices.

Proportionality. A recurring principle is that regulation should be proportionate to risk: a small start-up piloting a low-value product need not meet the same requirements as a large bank, but must respect core safeguards on consumer protection and anti-money-laundering.

sections.heading: 5.2 RegTech and Its Ecosystem
sections.html:
RegTech (regulatory technology) uses technology, such as automation, analytics and AI, to make regulatory compliance and reporting faster, cheaper and more reliable. Its regulator-side counterpart is SupTech (supervisory technology), which helps authorities collect and analyse data and monitor risk [1].

1
Capture data from all systems
→
2
Monitor in real time using rules and AI
→
3
Raise alerts on suspicious activity
→
4
File reports automatically (STR, CTR)
→
5
Supervisors review with SupTech tools

Fig. 1. RegTech workflow

Table 3. RegTech ecosystem

ParticipantRole
Regulated entities (banks, NBFCs, FinTechs)Adopt RegTech to meet obligations
RegTech vendorsSupply KYC, AML, reporting and risk tools
Regulators and supervisorsSet requirements; use SupTech for oversight
Auditors and consultantsValidate controls and processes
CustomersBenefit from smoother onboarding and safer services

Use cases of RegTech

Table 4. RegTech use cases

Use caseHow technology helps
Customer onboarding and KYCAutomated verification, liveness checks, document reading
Transaction monitoringRules and AI flag unusual patterns
Regulatory reportingAutomated data extraction and submission
Risk assessmentDashboards of credit, market and operational risk
Regulatory change managementTracks new circulars and maps them to internal policies
Complaint analysisText analytics identify recurring issues

Benefits and challenges

RegTech reduces cost, improves accuracy and speeds up reporting. Yet challenges persist: integrating with legacy systems, ensuring data quality, avoiding over-reliance on opaque models and ensuring that vendors themselves are secure and accountable. On the supervisory side, SupTech tools allow regulators to receive granular data in near real time and to identify emerging risks earlier [1].

Indian example: Automated monitoring at a bank

A bank's AML software scans all transactions, compares them with customer profiles and flags unusual patterns, such as many small deposits followed by a transfer abroad. Compliance officers review the alerts and file a Suspicious Transaction Report where needed, a task that would be impossible manually at the scale of millions of daily transactions.

sections.heading: 5.3 Financial Inclusion and Adoption
sections.html:
Financial inclusion means that individuals and businesses have access to useful, affordable financial products delivered responsibly. The World Bank's Global Findex database tracks account ownership, digital payments and savings across economies and highlights the role of digital technology in closing gaps [8].

In India, the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, launched in 2014, opened basic bank accounts at scale, and together with Aadhaar and mobile phones formed the JAM trinity. UPI, Direct Benefit Transfer and Account Aggregators build on this foundation. Yet account ownership is not the same as active use; dormant accounts, low literacy, language barriers and mistrust limit adoption.

Table 5. Barriers to adoption and responses

BarrierResponse
Low financial and digital literacyTraining, vernacular interfaces, business correspondents
Lack of trustStrong consumer protection, ombudsman, fraud prevention
Connectivity and device costsAffordable data, UPI on feature phones, assisted channels
Documentation gapseKYC, DigiLocker, simplified KYC for small accounts

Dimensions of financial inclusion

Table 6. Dimensions of financial inclusion

DimensionQuestion asked
AccessCan people open accounts and reach services?
UsageDo they actually use the accounts and products?
QualityAre services affordable, suitable and fair?
Welfare impactDo they improve resilience and livelihoods?

The Global Findex database highlights that holding an account is only the first step; frequent use for payments and savings brings real benefits [8]. Business correspondents, who serve as agents of banks in villages, play an important role in last-mile access, supported by technologies such as micro-ATMs and AePS.

Financial literacy and consumer awareness

Regulators and public institutions run awareness campaigns on safe digital practices, grievance channels and scams. Literacy programmes work best when delivered in local languages, through trusted community networks such as self-help groups and combined with simple, well-designed products.

sections.heading: 5.4 Challenges in FinTech Regulation
sections.html:
Regulators face a set of persistent difficulties. Pace: technology moves faster than legislation. Fragmentation: multiple regulators may have overlapping jurisdiction over a single product, such as a super-app offering payments, credit and investments. Cross-border activity: platforms and crypto assets operate beyond national boundaries. Data and cyber risk: large data pools attract attackers and misuse. Consumer harm: mis-selling, hidden charges and aggressive recovery practices in digital lending required intervention [9]. Adoption challenges on the demand side include the digital divide, low awareness and fraud that erodes trust.

Consumer protection issues

  • Dark patterns: interfaces that nudge users to accept costly or unsuitable products.
  • Opaque pricing: fees and interest not clearly disclosed.
  • Data misuse: collecting more data than necessary or sharing it without clear consent.
  • Weak grievance redress: no accessible way to complain or reverse fraudulent transactions.
  • Algorithmic bias: automated decisions that disadvantage certain groups.

Systemic and cross-border issues

Large platforms can become important to the functioning of the financial system, so their failure could spread widely. Cross-border services complicate jurisdiction and enforcement, which calls for cooperation among regulators and adoption of common standards [10]. Crypto assets are a prominent example where national differences create regulatory arbitrage.

Balancing act

Over-regulation can stifle useful innovation, while under-regulation can leave consumers exposed. Proportionate, risk-based rules and continuous dialogue between regulators and industry are the usual way forward.

sections.heading: 5.5 Role of the Central Bank
sections.html:
The Reserve Bank of India, established in 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, performs several roles relevant to FinTech [3].

Table 7. Roles of the RBI

RoleRelevance to FinTech
Monetary authorityControls liquidity and interest rates through tools such as the repo rate
Issuer of currencyResponsible for banknotes and for exploring the digital rupee (CBDC) [11]
Regulator of payment systemsAuthorises and oversees payment operators under the PSS Act, 2007
Supervisor of banks and NBFCsSets prudential, KYC and digital lending norms
Banker to government and banksOperates RTGS and other settlement systems
Consumer protectionIntegrated Ombudsman Scheme (2021) for complaints

Monetary and financial stability functions

Besides regulating, the central bank conducts monetary policy through instruments such as the policy repo rate and liquidity operations, acts as lender of last resort in stress and monitors financial stability. FinTech affects all of these: faster payments change liquidity patterns, digital lending alters credit transmission and CBDC could change how money circulates [11].

Payment system oversight

Under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, entities that operate payment systems must be authorised by the RBI, which sets requirements on capital, governance, security, data storage and customer protection, and can inspect and penalise violations [3]. The Integrated Ombudsman Scheme provides a single point for customers to lodge complaints against regulated entities.

The digital rupee

The RBI has piloted a wholesale and a retail digital rupee. Possible benefits include cheaper settlement, programmable features and offline use; design questions include privacy, the effect on bank deposits and interoperability with existing systems [11].

sections.heading: 5.6 RBI Regulatory Sandbox Framework
sections.html:
A regulatory sandbox is a controlled environment in which firms test innovative products with real customers under regulatory supervision, limited scale and agreed safeguards. The RBI issued its enabling framework in August 2019 and invited applications in thematic cohorts, with the first cohort on retail payments; later themes included cross-border payments, MSME lending and prevention of financial frauds [12].

1
Application under a theme
→
2
Evaluation of eligibility
→
3
Live testing with safeguards
→
4
Assessment of results
→
5
Exit: scale up or discontinue

Fig. 2. Stages of the RBI sandbox

Benefits. Regulators learn about new technology early; firms gain clarity and credibility; customers are protected by limits on scale and by disclosure. Limits. A sandbox is not a permanent exemption, and passing it does not guarantee a licence. Selection is competitive, and tests must have a clear consumer benefit.

Principles for sandbox participation

  • Genuine innovation: the product must be new or significantly different.
  • Consumer benefit: a clear benefit to customers or the system must be demonstrated.
  • Need for testing: a real regulatory or practical reason must exist for a controlled trial.
  • Readiness: the applicant should have capacity to test and an exit strategy.
  • Safeguards: limits on customers, volumes and exposure, with consent and disclosure.

International experience suggests that sandboxes help regulators learn and firms refine products, though they require resources and careful selection to avoid unfairness or regulatory capture [7]. In India, sandbox cohorts have been organised around themes so that testing addresses priority policy areas [12].

Indian example: Testing a new payment idea

A start-up proposing a novel offline payment method for rural areas applies in the retail payments cohort, tests it with a limited number of users for a few months under RBI-approved conditions, and then either launches formally or modifies the design based on findings.

sections.heading: 5.7 Anti-Money Laundering (AML)
sections.html:
Money laundering is the process of disguising the proceeds of crime so that they appear legitimate. In India, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) criminalises it and obliges banks, financial institutions and other reporting entities to maintain records and report certain transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit – India (FIU-IND) [13]. Global standards are set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) [14].

1
Placement: illegal cash enters the system
→
2
Layering: many transfers hide the trail
→
3
Integration: money appears legitimate

Fig. 3. Stages of money laundering

Typical red flags include structuring (splitting large sums into small deposits, sometimes called smurfing), transactions inconsistent with a customer's profile, use of shell companies, and rapid movement of funds through multiple accounts. Reporting entities file Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs), and Cash Transaction Reports (CTRs) for cash transactions above the prescribed threshold of Rs 10 lakh in a month. FinTech firms must build AML controls into onboarding and monitoring just as banks do.

Elements of an AML compliance programme

  1. Policy and governance: board-approved AML policy and a designated Principal Officer who reports suspicious activity.
  2. Risk assessment: assess risks by customer, product, geography and delivery channel.
  3. Customer due diligence: identify and verify customers and beneficial owners.
  4. Monitoring and reporting: detect unusual transactions and file reports with FIU-IND.
  5. Record keeping: retain records for the prescribed period.
  6. Training and independent audit: staff awareness and periodic testing of controls.

These elements follow the risk-based approach recommended by the Financial Action Task Force [14], and the obligations under the PMLA [13].

Virtual digital assets and AML

Cross-border and pseudonymous features make virtual assets attractive for laundering. Global standards require virtual asset service providers to apply KYC and to share originator and beneficiary information for transfers, known as the travel rule. In India, certain service providers dealing with virtual digital assets have been brought within the scope of PMLA obligations by notification, which means that they must register with FIU-IND and apply KYC and reporting [14].

Indian example: A mule account

Several unrelated persons deposit small amounts into one newly opened account, and the money is immediately transferred out to another state. Monitoring software flags the pattern and the bank files an STR.

sections.heading: 5.8 Know Your Client (KYC)
sections.html:
KYC norms require regulated entities to identify and verify customers, understand the nature of their business and monitor transactions. The RBI's Master Direction on KYC sets out the framework, including customer identification, customer due diligence (CDD), enhanced due diligence (EDD) for high-risk customers such as politically exposed persons (PEPs), identification of the beneficial owner of companies and trusts, and periodic updation of records [15].

Table 8. Elements of KYC

ElementMeaning
Customer Identification ProgrammeVerify identity and address using official documents or eKYC
Customer Due DiligenceUnderstand the customer, purpose of account and source of funds
Enhanced Due DiligenceExtra checks for high-risk customers and PEPs
Beneficial ownershipIdentify the natural person who ultimately controls an entity
Periodic updationRefresh records based on risk
CKYC and V-CIPShared KYC records and remote video verification

Balancing inclusion and control. Simplified KYC for small accounts and digital verification lower the barrier for low-income customers, while risk-based monitoring ensures that lighter onboarding does not become a loophole [15].

Levels of due diligence

Table 9. KYC treatment by customer category

CategoryTreatment
Low-risk and small accountsSimplified procedures with limits on balances and transactions
Regular customersFull KYC through documents, eKYC or V-CIP
High-risk customersEnhanced due diligence, senior approval and closer monitoring
Legal entities and trustsIdentify the beneficial owner and understand control structure

Digital KYC and re-KYC

The RBI allows KYC through digital methods, including a prescribed digital KYC process and video-based identification, subject to safeguards on liveness, location and audit trail. Regulated entities must periodically refresh KYC, with frequency linked to risk: higher-risk customers are reviewed more often than low-risk ones [15]. Customers should respond promptly to genuine re-KYC requests but remain wary of unsolicited links asking for documents, which are a common phishing method.

sections.heading: 5.9 Tax Issues: Assessment Year 2026-27
sections.html:
FinTech activity raises several tax questions: how to tax virtual digital assets, whether platform fees attract GST, how to tax cross-border digital services and how to exchange financial-account information with other countries. For Assessment Year 2026-27, relating to income of FY 2025-26 under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the principal rules are summarised below. The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from 1 April 2026 and uses a single Tax Year; readers should verify current provisions on the Income Tax Department website [16].

Table 10. Key tax issues for FinTech, AY 2026-27

IssuePosition
Income from transfer of VDAFlat 30 per cent under Section 115BBH plus surcharge and cess; only cost of acquisition deductible
Loss from VDANo set-off against other income
TDS on transfer of VDA1 per cent under Section 194S, subject to thresholds
ReportingSchedule VDA in the return; reporting by specified entities of crypto-asset transactions
Gift of VDATaxable for the recipient above the prescribed limit
GST on FinTech service feesGenerally 18 per cent on fees and commissions
Cross-border informationCommon Reporting Standard (CRS) provides automatic exchange of financial account information
1
Buy at Rs 1,00,000
→
2
Sell at Rs 1,40,000
→
3
Gain Rs 40,000
→
4
Tax Rs 12,000 plus 4% cess = Rs 12,480

Fig. 4. Worked example of VDA tax

Indian example: TDS credit

The platform deducts 1 per cent TDS on the sale value of Rs 1,40,000, that is Rs 1,400. The seller claims this as credit while filing the return for AY 2026-27 and pays the balance tax. If the seller had another crypto loss, it could not be set off against this gain.

Compliance steps for a taxpayer holding virtual digital assets

  1. Maintain complete records of acquisition cost, sale proceeds and dates for every transaction.
  2. Check the annual information statement and TDS credits shown for the year.
  3. Compute income for each transfer separately, without netting losses against gains from other assets.
  4. Report the income in the schedule meant for virtual digital assets in the return for AY 2026-27.
  5. Pay any balance tax with interest and file the return by the due date.

These steps reflect the framework described by the Income Tax Department for AY 2026-27 [16]. Professional advice is recommended for complex cases such as staking, airdrops or cross-border platforms.

Tax considerations for FinTech businesses

FinTech firms must consider GST on fees and commissions, TDS on payments to vendors and professionals, and transfer pricing where they transact with foreign group entities. Platform operators in some segments have reporting duties to the tax department. Because tax law changes frequently, firms embed tax checks into compliance calendars and use software to track deadlines.

Professional caution

Tax rules change frequently. This section is for study and is not tax advice; always check the latest Finance Act, circulars and the Income Tax Department notifications.

sections.heading: 5.10 Data Protection and Cyber Compliance
sections.html:
Because FinTech runs on personal and financial data, data protection law is central to compliance. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets out how organisations may process the digital personal data of individuals [6]. Its framework uses a few core ideas.

Table 11. Key concepts in the DPDP Act

ConceptMeaning
Data principalThe individual to whom the data relates
Data fiduciaryThe entity that decides the purpose and means of processing
ConsentFree, specific, informed and unambiguous agreement, which can be withdrawn
Consent managerA registered entity through which individuals can give, manage and withdraw consent
Purpose limitation and data minimisationProcess only data necessary for the stated purpose
Security safeguards and breach notificationProtect data and report breaches as required
Grievance redressA channel for individuals to raise complaints

Implications for FinTech. Firms must obtain valid consent, explain purposes in plain language, limit retention, secure data and respond to individual rights. The Account Aggregator framework already embodies consent-based design and offers a model for compliance [17]. Sector regulators such as the RBI add their own requirements, for example on storage of payment data in India [18].

Cyber compliance. Entities must follow incident-reporting directions issued by CERT-In, maintain logs, and implement controls aligned with frameworks such as NIST [19]. Boards are increasingly expected to oversee cyber and data risk as part of enterprise risk management.

Indian example: Consent in a lending journey

A borrower applies for a loan through an app. The app explains which data it needs, such as bank statements via an Account Aggregator, for what period and purpose, and obtains consent. If the borrower later withdraws consent, the app stops further use and retains only what the law requires.

Discussion

How should a FinTech balance personalisation, which needs data, with the principle of data minimisation?

sections.heading: Chapter Summary
sections.html:
Chapter summary

  • Regulation must balance innovation, consumer protection and stability
  • Several regulators share FinTech oversight; the lead depends on the activity
  • RegTech and SupTech automate compliance and supervision
  • The RBI sandbox enables safe, time-bound experimentation
  • AML and KYC protect the system from misuse and must be risk-based
  • For AY 2026-27, VDA gains face a flat 30% tax and 1% TDS without loss set-off

sections.heading: Review Questions
sections.html:
The questions follow the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create); the level is shown in italics after each question. Answer each in your own words, using the module and the Indian examples.

Short answer questions

  1. Name the principal regulators of FinTech in India and state the domain of each. (Remember)
  2. Define RegTech and SupTech. (Remember)
  3. State the three stages of money laundering. (Remember)
  4. Explain the purpose of the RBI Regulatory Sandbox. (Understand)
  5. Explain customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence. (Understand)
  6. Explain the terms data principal, data fiduciary and consent manager under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. (Understand)
  7. Explain the dimensions of financial inclusion. (Understand)
  8. A FinTech lender wants to onboard customers digitally. Identify the KYC and AML obligations it must meet. (Apply)
  9. A taxpayer traded virtual digital assets during FY 2025-26. List the compliance steps for AY 2026-27 without computing any amounts. (Apply)
  10. A start-up wants to test a new payment product with a limited set of users. Explain whether the sandbox route is suitable and why. (Apply)

Long answer questions

  1. Analyse the regulatory architecture for FinTech in India and compare it with approaches followed in other jurisdictions. (Analyse)
  2. Examine the RegTech ecosystem, its benefits and challenges, and the role of SupTech. (Analyse)
  3. Evaluate the state of financial inclusion and adoption in India, discuss the challenges and recommend policy responses. (Evaluate)
  4. Explain the roles of the Reserve Bank of India and discuss how FinTech and the digital rupee affect them. (Analyse)
  5. Evaluate the AML and KYC regimes for digital finance, with reference to the risk-based approach and the need to balance inclusion with control. (Evaluate)
  6. Develop a compliance framework for a new FinTech platform covering licensing, KYC and AML, data protection, cyber-security and tax for AY 2026-27. (Create)

sections.heading: Glossary
sections.html:
TermMeaning
Regulatory sandboxA controlled environment for testing innovative products under supervision with limited scale and safeguards.
RegTechTechnology used by firms to automate regulatory compliance and reporting.
SupTechTechnology used by supervisors to collect and analyse data and monitor risk.
Financial inclusionAccess to and use of affordable, suitable financial services by all sections of society.
Business correspondentAn agent of a bank who delivers services in areas without branches.
PSS Act, 2007The law under which payment systems in India are authorised and regulated by the RBI.
Integrated Ombudsman SchemeThe RBI's single-window scheme for customer complaints against regulated entities.
PMLAThe Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.
FIU-INDThe Financial Intelligence Unit of India, which receives reports of suspicious and large transactions.
FATFThe global standard setter for anti-money-laundering and counter-terror-financing.
Placement, layering, integrationThe three stages by which illegal funds are introduced, disguised and made to appear legitimate.
STR / CTRSuspicious Transaction Report and Cash Transaction Report.
KYCKnow Your Customer norms for verifying identity and understanding customers.
CDD / EDDCustomer Due Diligence and Enhanced Due Diligence for high-risk customers.
PEPPolitically Exposed Person who needs closer scrutiny.
Beneficial ownerThe natural person who ultimately owns or controls an entity.
DPDP Act, 2023India's law governing the processing of digital personal data.
Data fiduciaryAn entity that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data.
Consent managerA registered entity that helps individuals give, manage and withdraw consent.
CERT-InIndia's national agency for responding to cyber-security incidents.
Tax YearThe single period used for tax purposes under the Income-tax Act, 2025, replacing previous year and assessment year.
Schedule VDAThe part of the income-tax return used to report income from virtual digital assets.
